# Carpal tunnel syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Carpal tunnel syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/sR0tof)

---

## Summary

<u>Carpal tunnel</u> syndrome (CTS) is a <u>peripheral neuropathy</u> caused by chronic or acute compression of the <u>median nerve</u> under the <u>transverse carpal ligament</u>. CTS is the most common form of <u>entrapment neuropathy</u>, a group that includes <u>cubital tunnel syndrome</u>, <u>radiculopathies</u>, and <u>tarsal tunnel syndrome</u>. It is characterized by both sensory disturbances (<u>pain</u>, tingling, and numbness) and motor symptoms (weakened <u>thenar muscles</u> leading to weakened pinch and grip of the thumb) in the area innervated by the <u>median nerve</u> <u>distal</u> to the <u>carpal tunnel</u>. Several occupational and nonoccupational <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., manual <u>labor</u>, age, sex, <u>diabetes</u>) have been associated with CTS. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by symptoms and results of <u>provocative tests for CTS</u> (e.g., <u>hand elevation test</u>, <u>carpal compression test</u>, and <u>Phalen test</u>). Additional testing (e.g., <u>electrodiagnostic studies</u>) is indicated if there is diagnostic uncertainty. Patients with mild to moderate symptoms are generally <u>managed conservatively</u> (e.g., <u>immobilization</u> with a <u>splint</u>, local <u>steroid</u> injections). Surgical release of the <u>transverse carpal ligament</u> with decompression of the <u>median nerve</u> may be indicated for patients with severe disease (e.g., <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>thenar eminence</u>) or symptoms refractory to <u>conservative treatment</u>.

---

## Etiology

CTS is caused by compression of the <u>median nerve</u> in the <u>carpal tunnel</u>, under the <u>transverse carpal ligament</u>. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[3]](/library/5j0iaT)[[4]](/library/Kl1UBS0)




* Previous <u>fracture</u> of the wrist

* Traumatic <u>dislocation</u> of the lunate [[5]](/library/561il30)

* Manual work:  increased risk in workers using vibrating tools or prolonged, forceful, and repetitive <u>flexion</u>/extension of the wrist [[6]](/library/Mj0MaT)

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u> and other types of <u>chronic inflammation</u> of the <u>tendon sheaths</u> [[3]](/library/5j0iaT)

* <u>Pregnancy</u> and <u>puerperium</u>  [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>Systemic amyloidosis</u>

* <u>Renal failure</u> and dialysis-associated deposition of <u>amyloid</u> [[4]](/library/Kl1UBS0)[[8]](/library/BVXz9C)

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>  [[9]](/library/Kj0UYT)

* <u>Acromegaly</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>carpal tunnel</u> is a narrow fibro-osseous structure at the level of the <u>palmar</u> aspect of the wrist, delimited by the <u>carpal bones</u> and the <u>transverse carpal ligament</u>, which contains flexor <u>tendons</u> and the <u>median nerve</u>.

* Pressure increase within the <u>carpal tunnel</u> → compression of contained structures → impaired blood flow and altered <u>microvascular</u> structure of the <u>median nerve</u> → inflammatory reaction → <u>edema</u> and <u>hypoxia</u> → axonal degeneration [[10]](/library/6j0jYT)[[11]](/library/qj0CYT)

## Clinical features

### Symptoms [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Develop in the areas innervated by the <u>median nerve</u>: <u>palmar</u> surface of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, and radial half of the ring finger.

* <u>Paresthesia</u>: burning sensation, tingling

* Loss of sensation/numbness

* <u>Pain</u>: may radiate to the forearm and/or upper arm

* Typically worsen at night

* Patients often report that symptoms improve by shaking the hand (flick sign).  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Severely affected patients may report:

* Dropping objects;  and difficulty with fine motor skills (e.g., buttoning up clothing) secondary to weakened finger pinch and grip strength

* Disappearance of <u>pain</u>  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)





> [!TIP]
> Motor deficits are typically only seen in severe disease. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




### Examination findings [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Mild disease: Initial examination is often normal; symptoms only develop with <u>provocative tests for CTS</u>.

* Severe disease: Findings of both sensory and motor deficits may be seen. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* <u>Examination of the sensory system</u>

* May show decreased sensation in the area innervated by the <u>median nerve</u> <u>distal</u> to the <u>carpal tunnel</u>   [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Usually, there is no loss of sensation of the <u>palmar</u> surface of the <u>thenar eminence</u> because it is innervated by the <u>superficial</u> branch of the <u>median nerve</u>, which arises 5–7 cm <u>proximal</u> to the <u>carpal tunnel</u> and is, therefore, not compressed.  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* <u>Examination of the motor system</u>: may show <u>weakness</u> in thumb <u>abduction</u> and opposition as well as thenar <u>atrophy</u>   [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)





> [!TIP]
> Sensory innervation of the <u>thenar eminence</u> is not affected in CTS.




> [!NOTE]
> The "<u>pope's blessing</u>" (inability to flex the first three digits when making a fist) is not a symptom of CTS. It is only seen in <u>proximal</u> lesions of the <u>median nerve</u>




> [!WARNING]
> Examine the entire upper limb to rule out <u>differential diagnoses of CTS</u>. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Usually a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, based on classic <u>clinical features of CTS</u> combined with positive <u>provocative tests for CTS</u>  [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)

* Consider additional testing (e.g., <u>electrodiagnostic studies</u>, imaging) in:

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Severe cases (e.g., those that may require surgical intervention)





### Provocative tests for CTS [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Overview

* Considered positive when sensory symptoms (e.g., <u>pain</u>, <u>paresthesias</u>) are elicited along the distribution of the <u>median nerve</u> <u>distal</u> to the <u>carpal tunnel</u> [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Usually performed in combination as use of a single provocative test has low <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>  [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Commonly used provocation tests

* Phalen test: The patient's wrist is held in full <u>flexion</u> (90°) for one minute.   [[13]](/library/ql1CBS0)

* Tinel sign: The examiner percusses or taps with the fingertips over the <u>carpal tunnel</u>.

* Hand elevation test: The patient holds both hands above their head for one minute.

* Carpal compression test: The examiner uses a finger to apply moderate pressure directly over the <u>carpal tunnel</u> for 30 seconds.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not use a single provocative test to diagnose CTS; using a combination of tests increases diagnostic <u>accuracy</u>. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)

### <u>Electrophysiological tests</u> [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Indications [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Diagnostic uncertainty or atypical presentation [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)

* To rule out alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>polyneuropathy</u>, <u>radiculopathy</u>)

* Presurgical evaluation  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Modalities

* <u>Nerve conduction studies</u> (<u>confirmatory test</u>): show impaired <u>median nerve</u> conduction along the <u>carpal tunnel</u> [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Prolonged sensory and <u>distal motor latency</u> [[14]](/library/Ck1qJS0)

* May be normal in patients with mild disease

* <u>Electromyogram</u> [[15]](/library/xk1EJS0)

* Usually ordered to rule out alternative diagnoses

* May show abnormal spontaneous activity (e.g., fibrillation potentials) or altered <u>action potential</u> morphology [[14]](/library/Ck1qJS0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Electrodiagnostic studies</u> are not necessary to confirm a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> of CTS but should be ordered when the diagnosis is uncertain and for patients scheduled to have <u>surgery</u>. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




### Additional evaluation [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)[[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)




* Imaging: Consider if structural abnormalities or alternative diagnoses are suspected. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)[[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)

* First line: <u>x-ray</u> wrist to rule out bony pathology [[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)

* If <u>x-ray</u> is normal, consider <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> without IV contrast.  [[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)

* Findings include increased cross-sectional area of the <u>median nerve</u> and nerve flattening. [[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)

* Can also help to evaluate for <u>tenosynovitis</u> and mass lesions [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)[[16]](/library/Bk1zJS0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: Consider based on clinical features, e.g., <u>screening for diabetes</u> or <u>thyroid function tests</u>. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

## Treatment

### Approach [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Mild to moderate disease [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Trial <u>immobilization</u> or <u>glucocorticoid</u> injection.

* No response after 6 weeks  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Assess for adherence.

* Trial alternate conservative methods.

* Severe or refractory disease: Refer to a hand specialist for possible <u>surgery</u>. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)





### <u>Conservative management</u> [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Treatment of underlying comorbidities: see “<u>Etiology of CTS</u>.”

* <u>Immobilization</u>: splinting of the wrist in a neutral position.  [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)[[17]](/library/aL1Qwh0)

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* First-line: <u>steroid</u> injection, e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Consider <u>ultrasound</u> guidance to reduce the risk of nerve or <u>tendon</u> injury.

* A single injection can provide symptomatic relief lasting from 10 weeks to 1 year.  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Alternative: oral <u>glucocorticoids</u>, e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Should only be used short-term (e.g., 2–4 weeks); monitor for <u>side effects of glucocorticoid therapy</u>. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* Can provide up to 8 weeks of symptomatic relief [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

* <u>Physical therapy</u> and exercise: e.g., nerve glide exercises, <u>therapeutic ultrasound</u>, and <u>carpal bone mobilization</u>  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Oral analgesia</u> (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>gabapentin</u>) is not effective in managing CTS. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




### <u>Surgery</u> [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)[[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)




* Indications: severe disease or refractory symptoms

* Method

* Open or endoscopic release of the <u>transverse carpal ligament</u>  [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)[[15]](/library/xk1EJS0)

* The <u>transverse carpal ligament</u> is divided to increase space for the <u>median nerve</u> in the <u>carpal tunnel</u>. [[15]](/library/xk1EJS0)

* Follow-up

* <u>Immobilization</u> is not recommended after <u>surgery</u>. [[2]](/library/Nj1-0S0)

* Most patients return to normal activities within 2 weeks. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)





> [!TIP]
> Patients with severe disease may not fully recover function but <u>nerve conduction studies</u> should show an improvement. [[12]](/library/mj1VaS0)

## Special patient groups

### Carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)




* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)[[19]](/library/nj17aS0)

* Most commonly seen <u>entrapment neuropathy</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)

* Occurs in up to 62% of pregnant women [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)

* Etiology [[19]](/library/nj17aS0)

* <u>Hormone</u>-mediated changes [[20]](/library/QO1uHS0)

* Weight gain and fluid retention [[19]](/library/nj17aS0)

* Changes to the <u>musculoskeletal system</u>  [[19]](/library/nj17aS0)

* <u>Edema</u> of the wrist

* <u>Gestational diabetes</u>

* <u>Gestational hypertension</u>

* Clinical features [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)

* Similar to the general population (see “<u>Clinical features of CTS</u>”)

* Patients commonly present in the <u>third trimester</u> (but can present at any stage).

* Often bilateral

* Modifications to <u>diagnostics of CTS</u>: none

* Modifications to <u>treatment of CTS</u>

* <u>Conservative management</u> is recommended during <u>pregnancy</u> as symptoms often resolve after delivery. [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)[[21]](/library/5j1iaS0)

* <u>Surgery</u> may be required if symptoms persist postpartum.  [[7]](/library/Nmc-f10)[[22]](/library/PO1WsS0)
